newsitem.title: USA: Hewlett-Packard to unveil powerful servers.
newsitem.headline: Hewlett-Packard to unveil powerful servers.

text.p: Hewlett-Packard Co. will launch a powerful high-end computer and other products Thursday in a bid to regain the momentum from fast-charging rival Sun Microsystems Inc., analysts said.

Senior executives from HP, whose shares were dented last week after it turned in a fiscal second quarter report that fell short of Wall Street expectations, were also due to face investor scrutiny at an analyst meeting in New York City.
HP must shake off a perception that it has been muddling through a series of product transitions while the rest of the industry is moving ahead at warp speed, analysts said.

"HP's lost momentum," said Andrew Allison, a Carmel, California-based computer industry consultant and editor of Inside the New Computer Industry. "There is a chance Sun can overtake them, but I wouldn't count them out yet."

The showcase item of Hewlett-Packard's new products announcement, set for noon EST (1600 GMT) in Manhattan, is a new range of high-end V Series computers developed with technology from its Convex Computer Corp. subsidiary.

The V Series computers will be pitched as alternatives to mainframe computers of the variety made by industry giant International Business Machines Corp.. HP unplugged the last of its own mainframe computers just a year ago.

This is the same market targeted by Sun Microsystems' Ultra Enterprise 10000 machines, codenamed Starfire, launched in January. The Sun machines recently hit full production and have been so successful that output has already been raised.
Analysts see HP's new V Series as a direct strike against Sun, and they expect it to show significant benchmark records using HP's latest Precision Architecture 8200 processors.
"It's going to leapfrog Sun Microsystems' Ultra Enterprise server," predicted David Wu, an analyst at ABN AMRO Chicago Corp.
Sun will not stand idly by, however, said Shahin Khan, director of marketing for Sun's Starfire business.
"You can expect enhancements across the board" to Sun's top-end systems, he said in an interview.

HP executives have voiced irritation over the recent progress of Sun, which has shifted its business towards servers, which run vast networks of computers, from the higher end desktop machines used by engineers known as workstations.
Sun's revenues are roughly one-fifth of HP's fiscal 1996 revenues of $38.4 billion.

Nevertheless, Sun's year-on-year midrange server revenue growth rate is estimated at 287 percent, acccording to International Data Corp, a research group that projects Sun will continue to gain market share in 1997 and 1998.
Some analysts wonder if HP isn't faced with the prospect of a growth plateau similar to that experienced by IBM in the late 1980s when its earnings stagnated.
"Just in the computer business, they've got half a dozen multi-billion-dollar businesses to manage, and it's a competitive world out there," one said.
HP reported orders in its second quarter ended April 30 rose just three percent, against the previous quarter's double-digit growth, and fell two percent in the U.S. market.
